paper.title: Contents
paper.abstract: Abstract Accurate prediction does not establish that a world model has recovered a physical law: distinct dynamics can generate identical records under the same observation protocol. We formulate law recovery on a fixed physical domain under an explicit catalog of experiments, sensor uncertainty, and an acquisition budget. A rate–distortion converse separates the information needed to describe a law from the information the apparatus can reveal. Its constructive counterpart gives a finite response codebook and an explicit decoding budget. On compact world classes, uniform recovery is possible exactly when every pair of different laws is experimentally distinguishable; equivalently, the apparatus can recover all the entropy of every finite law source. An inverse response modulus quantifies stability. For Lipschitz fields on a d d -dimensional state–action domain, noisy full-state readouts after resets require minimax budget Θ ( ε − ( d + 4 ) / 2 ) \Theta(\varepsilon^{-(d+4)/2}) for squared law error ε \varepsilon , compared with Θ ( ε − ( d + 2 ) / 2 ) \Theta(\varepsilon^{-(d+2)/2}) for direct field observations. Exact crossing-time symmetries establish the lower bound under adaptive experiment selection and arbitrary durations with constant inputs. Reproducible synthetic cases illustrate the separate roles of intervention, calibration, and repeated measurement. Together, the results identify which evidence supports a claim of physical-law recovery and the cost of acquiring it.

sections.heading: 1  Introduction
sections.text: An agent that acts in a physical environment must anticipate the consequences of its actions. Before moving an object, changing a machine setting, or applying a force, it benefits from knowing what is likely to happen next. A world model provides such predictions from previous observations and actions. The scientific question considered in this report begins one step further: when do the observations support recovery of the physical law that generates those consequences? We ask what an experiment must reveal, how accurately the law can then be recovered, and what acquiring that evidence costs. The distinction can be understood without choosing a learning algorithm. Suppose a model predicts the next position of a moving object accurately throughout a recording. This establishes agreement with the observed motion. It does not yet establish what the object would do from another initial position, at another velocity, or under an intervention absent from the recording. A physical law makes these additional predictions through a common rule of evolution. Recovering that rule therefore requires deciding between explanations that agree on the available observations but differ on the physical situations of interest. More examples of the same motion need not resolve the decision. Consider an object moving around a fixed center, as in Figure 1 . One candidate law is inverse-square attraction: the acceleration magnitude decreases as the square of the distance increases. Another is a linear restoring law: the acceleration magnitude increases in proportion to distance. Choose units in which both laws give unit inward acceleration at unit radius. Its initial inward acceleration is now 1 / 4 1/4 under inverse-square attraction and 2 2 under the restoring law, so the position responses separate. This is a change in preparation, not an external force applied during the motion. Repeating the circular record only refines an already shared prediction; repeating the release can distinguish the two explanations despite measurement noise. The example will recur throughout the report, first as a recovery problem, then as an information constraint, and finally as a concrete experiment with a calculable error probability. For this example, the physical state is position and velocity together, x = ( 𝒒 , 𝒗 ) x=(\bm{q},\bm{v}) , and the corresponding first-order laws are F G ​ ( x ) = ( 𝒗 , a G ​ ( 𝒒 ) ) F_{G}(x)=(\bm{v},a_{G}(\bm{q})) and F H ​ ( x ) = ( 𝒗 , a H ​ ( 𝒒 ) ) F_{H}(x)=(\bm{v},a_{H}(\bm{q})) . More generally, we study a field F F in an ordinary differential equation x ˙ = F ⁡ ( x , u ) \dot{x}=F(x,u) , where u u denotes a controlled input when one is available. Recovery means estimating this field over a declared physical domain. It does not require discovering a unique symbolic expression: different expressions can define the same field. It does require specifying the coordinates, region, and accuracy in which two candidate fields are to be compared. This question complements the predictive use of world models. Ha and Schmidhuber (2018) learned compact representations of environments for control, and PlaNet planned through learned latent dynamics from image observations ( Hafner et al., 2019 ) . Dreamer subsequently demonstrated the usefulness of world models across diverse control tasks ( Hafner et al., 2025 ) . These results make prediction and planning compelling objectives in their own right. Our concern is the additional evidence needed when a model is interpreted as recovering a physical rule. A representation useful for choosing actions need not uniquely determine the continuous-time field in specified physical coordinates. Related distinctions arise in representation learning. I-JEPA predicts representations of unobserved image regions from visible context, while V-JEPA learns from predicting features of video ( Assran et al., 2023 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ) . Such objectives can learn useful abstractions without reconstructing every observed detail. They do not, by themselves, specify a physical-coordinate recovery target or an experiment that identifies it. In another setting, Locatello et al. (2019) showed that unsupervised disentanglement requires assumptions on models and data. Causal representation learning likewise asks how learned variables can support a causal description ( Schölkopf et al., 2021 ) . These questions concern latent representations rather than the dynamical fields studied here, but they reinforce the need to specify what fixes the physical meaning of an estimate. Our coordinates and sensing assumptions are explicit parts of the recovery problem. The issue has a long history in system identification. Structural identifiability asks whether different systems can generate the same observations ( Bellman and Åström, 1970 ) ; symmetries of dynamics and sensing explain why such equivalences can persist ( Sontag, 2017 ) . In the circular example, the available motion never visits radii where the laws differ. With an uncertain sensor, an additional ambiguity is possible: changing the physical scale while compensating through sensor gain can leave all readings unchanged. The report treats both as properties of the permitted experiments. An informative release addresses the first obstruction; a known physical reference may be necessary for the second. Recovering equations from data also builds on substantial constructive work. The sparse Bayesian approach of Pan et al. (2016) identifies nonlinear state-space systems using sparse structure; SINDy applies similar idea by selecting governing terms from a candidate library ( Brunton et al., 2016 ) . Neural ordinary differential equations instead parameterize continuous-time dynamics through trainable vector fields ( Chen et al., 2018 ) . Active identification provides guarantees for nonlinear dynamics linear in known features ( Mania et al., 2022 ) , and continuous-time sampling theory characterizes when sampled evolution determines its generator ( Zeng et al., 2024 ) . These methods and results answer different parts of the recovery problem. Our formulation makes the target domain, sensor uncertainty, executable interventions, and acquisition costs explicit within a common analysis. The starting point is thus the experimental record, before selecting a representation or optimizer. An apparatus supplies a catalog of operations: preparing states, applying specified inputs, observing at chosen times, and, when available, calibrating against a reference. A learner may choose the next operation using earlier readings. Every operation has a cost, and the complete record must fit an acquisition budget. The central difficulty is whether this record separates candidate laws to the required physical precision. This perspective permits limits that apply to every learning algorithm, together with constructions that show when those limits can be approached. Information theory provides a useful language for separating the demands of the target from the abilities of the apparatus ( Shannon, 1948 ; Shannon, 1959 ; Cover and Thomas, 2006 ) . A law class may contain many physically different possibilities at a given resolution; describing the correct one requires information. Experiments deliver information through their responses. In the equal-prior two-law example, identifying the correct candidate requires one bit, but the circular experiment reveals none of it. The release can reveal that distinction. With a continuous law class, metric entropy and rate–distortion quantify the corresponding description requirement, while experimental information capacity describes what can be learned within the budget. There is an essential difference from ordinary communication. An experimenter does not know the true law and cannot encode it freely into a channel input. The experimenter can only probe the unknown world using available operations. Consequently, an inequality comparing required and available information is a necessary condition; it does not alone construct a successful recovery procedure. We give a separate response-matching decoder based on a finite collection of representative worlds. Under the stated compactness and continuity assumptions, arbitrary uniform accuracy is possible exactly when every pair of different target laws can be separated by some permitted experiment. The separating program may depend on the requested precision. Accuracy also depends on how strongly responses separate. Closely spaced responses require more repetitions in noise, and a small response error can correspond to a large physical-law error. Our analysis uses established tools from minimax information bounds, sequential experimental design, and inverse-problem stability ( Yang and Barron, 1999 ; Yu, 1997 ; Chernoff, 1959 ; Kaufmann et al., 2016 ; Donoho and Liu, 1991 ; Donoho, 1994 ) . For a concrete class of Lipschitz fields, we then quantify how preparation, readout, and elapsed time determine acquisition cost. The squared-error exponent − 2 / ( d + 4 ) -2/(d+4) is already established for nonparametric ODE estimation under specified observation designs ( Schötz, 2026 ; Schötz and Siebel, 2026 ) ; our costed access model examines it with adaptive experiment selection and contrasts state observations with direct field observations. The argument proceeds in this order. Section 2 defines the physical target and available experiments. Section 3 asks which laws those experiments can separate. Section 4 compares description requirements with accessible information, and Section 5 constructs a decoder and explains its stability. Section 6 specializes the theory to acquisition costs for Lipschitz dynamics. Section 7 returns to the orbital example and adds calibration and noisy-estimation cases. Each stage addresses a question left open by the previous one: what is being recovered, whether the evidence determines it, how accurately it can be recovered, and how much that accuracy costs.

Section 5 will show why compactness turns this pairwise condition into uniform recovery at every positive tolerance. We now turn from distinctions that are absent to distinctions that must be measured accurately. This requires a measure of the information needed to describe the law and a separate measure of the information the apparatus can reveal.

sections.text: Shannon’s theory separates the information required to describe a source from the information a channel can convey ( Shannon, 1948 ; Shannon, 1959 ) . For physical-law learning, these are different objects: complexity belongs to the target field on D D , while accessible information belongs to the experiments and their sensors. We first consider the description of a law at finite resolution, then allow an average reconstruction error, and finally ask what information can be obtained from actual experiments. If there were only finitely many candidate laws, naming one would require an index into that finite set. The construction treats a world as a joint hypothesis about dynamics and sensing, because the same physical field can produce different responses under different sensors. Its output is only the physical field. The idea is to list finitely many representative responses, repeat a program that separates physically different laws, and return the field whose representative response best matches the observed average. sections.heading: 8  Consequences and Scope
sections.text: The theory separates three questions. Rate–distortion describes the information required for a specified physical fidelity. Experimental completeness asks whether the apparatus can reveal the relevant distinctions. Inverse stability and acquisition cost determine how accurately they can be measured. A low prediction loss becomes evidence of physical recovery only when the target domain, observation model, and experimental access connect it to that claim. Several consequences follow. Additional observations of an equivalent world pair cannot remove its law ambiguity. More expressive models cannot distinguish identical transcript distributions. Excitation and calibration solve different problems: excitation changes which dynamics are revealed, while calibration can anchor their physical coordinates. Even a correctly identified sampled transition map need not uniquely identify a continuous-time generator without suitable sampling assumptions ( Zeng et al., 2024 ) . These are failures of particular implications, rather than claims that predictive world models are ineffective for their intended control tasks. The running example gives these conclusions an operational meaning. An evaluation set containing only the observed circular motion rewards both laws equally. A region containing other radii asks a question the same data cannot answer. Releasing the object changes the evidence while keeping the physical target fixed. Moving the release point or readout time changes the strength and price of that evidence. The progression is from deciding which physical distinctions matter, to making them observable, to measuring them precisely. A larger training set helps at the last step only if its acquisition protocol supports the earlier ones. Recovering a field also differs from discovering a preferred symbolic expression. The loss in ( 2 ) compares physical derivatives over D D . Two expressions defining the same field there have zero distance, and extensions differing only outside D D are not separated. The results support a specified domain of physical validity. They do not assert that a finite experiment uniquely selects a universal formula or an internal neural representation. Symbolic, numerical, and learned representations can thus be judged against the same physical question while retaining their distinct representational aims. The response-codebook construction offers a way to understand what a learned predictor would have to accomplish. Its observations must resolve candidate fields at the requested physical accuracy; its representation must retain the distinctions needed by the decoder; and its approximation and optimization errors must fit within the remaining error allowance. The present theorems establish statistical possibility by constructing one decoder. Applying them to a particular encoder, latent transition model, and decoder requires an additional argument linking that implementation to physical-coordinate field error. The continuous-force example makes one part of this issue visible: repeating an informative experiment reduces measurement noise, whereas refining a fixed response codebook reduces its approximation error. These operations address different contributions to the reconstruction error. Unknown sensing makes the physical-coordinate requirement especially consequential. In the gain example, an entire family of different physical gains produces the same observable dynamics. A known-state reference anchors the missing scale. If such references are unavailable, one may instead seek a model of observable dynamics or a law defined only up to the unresolved coordinate transformation. That is a legitimate alternative target, but its equivalence relation and loss must be stated accordingly. It cannot be converted into the fixed-coordinate recovery claim merely by attaching physical names to latent variables. The formulation makes the required references explicit rather than assigning them implicitly to the representation. The results are statistical guarantees for a correctly specified compact world class, repeatable world-independent Gaussian noise, and the declared apparatus. The constructive codebook can be computationally prohibitive, and its sufficient budget need not match the information converse for every apparatus. Physical-coordinate recovery requires the necessary physical references; arbitrary latent coordinates and passive video are not covered by the sufficient access conditions. The nonparametric budget theorem measures the entire first-order state, fixes constant actions during each episode, and assumes strictly positive noise. Smoother classes, partial-state observations, model misspecification, and control waveforms within episodes require separate analyses. The simulations isolate these mechanisms in small systems and do not establish an advantage for any neural architecture. The central claim is therefore operational: a world model can be certified as a recovered physical law only relative to a stated target and experiments capable of separating its competing explanations. This perspective makes the acquisition protocol part of the learning problem and exposes the cost of turning predictive evidence into physical knowledge.

Ye Yuan 1 and Jun Liu 2 1 School of Artificial Intelligence and Automation, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China yye@hust.edu.cn 2 Department of Applied Mathematics, University of Waterloo, Waterloo, Canada j.liu@uwaterloo.ca 15 September 2026 Abstract Accurate prediction does not establish that a world model has recovered a physical law: distinct dynamics can generate identical records under the same observation protocol. We formulate law recovery on a fixed physical domain under an explicit catalog of experiments, sensor uncertainty, and an acquisition budget. A rate–distortion converse separates the information needed to describe a law from the information the apparatus can reveal. Its constructive counterpart gives a finite response codebook and an explicit decoding budget. On compact world classes, uniform recovery is possible exactly when every pair of different laws is experimentally distinguishable; equivalently, the apparatus can recover all the entropy of every finite law source. An inverse response modulus quantifies stability. For Lipschitz fields on a d d -dimensional state–action domain, noisy full-state readouts after resets require minimax budget Θ ( ε − ( d + 4 ) / 2 ) \Theta(\varepsilon^{-(d+4)/2}) for squared law error ε \varepsilon , compared with Θ ( ε − ( d + 2 ) / 2 ) \Theta(\varepsilon^{-(d+2)/2}) for direct field observations. Exact crossing-time symmetries establish the lower bound under adaptive experiment selection and arbitrary durations with constant inputs. Reproducible synthetic cases illustrate the separate roles of intervention, calibration, and repeated measurement. Together, the results identify which evidence supports a claim of physical-law recovery and the cost of acquiring it. 1 Introduction An agent that acts in a physical environment must anticipate the consequences of its actions. Before moving an object, changing a machine setting, or applying a force, it benefits from knowing what is likely to happen next. A world model provides such predictions from previous observations and actions. The scientific question considered in this report begins one step further: when do the observations support recovery of the physical law that generates those consequences? We ask what an experiment must reveal, how accurately the law can then be recovered, and what acquiring that evidence costs. The distinction can be understood without choosing a learning algorithm. Suppose a model predicts the next position of a moving object accurately throughout a recording. This establishes agreement with the observed motion. It does not yet establish what the object would do from another initial position, at another velocity, or under an intervention absent from the recording. A physical law makes these additional predictions through a common rule of evolution. Recovering that rule therefore requires deciding between explanations that agree on the available observations but differ on the physical situations of interest. More examples of the same motion need not resolve the decision. Consider an object moving around a fixed center, as in Figure 1 . One candidate law is inverse-square attraction: the acceleration magnitude decreases as the square of the distance increases. Another is a linear restoring law: the acceleration magnitude increases in proportion to distance. Choose units in which both laws give unit inward acceleration at unit radius. The accelerations at planar position 𝒒  m{q} are then a G ( 𝒒 ) = − 𝒒 / ∥ 𝒒 ∥ 3 a_{G}( m{q})=- m{q}/\| m{q}\|^{3} and a H ​ ( 𝒒 ) = − 𝒒 a_{H}( m{q})=- m{q} . Start the object at unit radius with unit tangential speed. Both laws produce exactly the same circular motion, with the same position at every time. Even an arbitrarily long, noiseless recording cannot identify which law generated it. Figure 1: Why accurate prediction of a recorded motion need not identify its physical law. This is a change in preparation, not an external force applied during the motion. Repeating the circular record only refines an already shared prediction; repeating the release can distinguish the two explanations despite measurement noise. The example will recur throughout the report, first as a recovery problem, then as an information constraint, and finally as a concrete experiment with a calculable error probability. For this example, the physical state is position and velocity together, x = ( 𝒒 , 𝒗 ) x=( m{q}, m{v}) , and the corresponding first-order laws are F G ​ ( x ) = ( 𝒗 , a G ​ ( 𝒒 ) ) F_{G}(x)=( m{v},a_{G}( m{q})) and F H ​ ( x ) = ( 𝒗 , a H ​ ( 𝒒 ) ) F_{H}(x)=( m{v},a_{H}( m{q})) . More generally, we study a field F F in an ordinary differential equation x ˙ = F ⁡ ( x , u ) \dot{x}=F(x,u) , where u u denotes a controlled input when one is available. Recovery means estimating this field over a declared physical domain. It does not require discovering a unique symbolic expression: different expressions can define the same field. It does require specifying the coordinates, region, and accuracy in which two candidate fields are to be compared. This question complements the predictive use of world models. Ha and Schmidhuber (2018) learned compact representations of environments for control, and PlaNet planned through learned latent dynamics from image observations ( Hafner et al., 2019 ) . Dreamer subsequently demonstrated the usefulness of world models across diverse control tasks ( Hafner et al., 2025 ) . These results make prediction and planning compelling objectives in their own right. Our concern is the additional evidence needed when a model is interpreted as recovering a physical rule. A representation useful for choosing actions need not uniquely determine the continuous-time field in specified physical coordinates. Related distinctions arise in representation learning. I-JEPA predicts representations of unobserved image regions from visible context, while V-JEPA learns from predicting features of video ( Assran et al., 2023 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ) . Such objectives can learn useful abstractions without reconstructing every observed detail. They do not, by themselves, specify a physical-coordinate recovery target or an experiment that identifies it. In another setting, Locatello et al. (2019) showed that unsupervised disentanglement requires assumptions on models and data. Causal representation learning likewise asks how learned variables can support a causal description ( Schölkopf et al., 2021 ) . These questions concern latent representations rather than the dynamical fields studied here, but they reinforce the need to specify what fixes the physical meaning of an estimate. Our coordinates and sensing assumptions are explicit parts of the recovery problem. The issue has a long history in system identification. Structural identifiability asks whether different systems can generate the same observations ( Bellman and Åström, 1970 ) ; symmetries of dynamics and sensing explain why such equivalences can persist ( Sontag, 2017 ) . In the circular example, the available motion never visits radii where the laws differ. With an uncertain sensor, an additional ambiguity is possible: changing the physical scale while compensating through sensor gain can leave all readings unchanged. The report treats both as properties of the permitted experiments. An informative release addresses the first obstruction; a known physical reference may be necessary for the second. Recovering equations from data also builds on substantial constructive work. The sparse Bayesian approach of Pan et al. (2016) identifies nonlinear state-space systems using sparse structure; SINDy applies similar idea by selecting governing terms from a candidate library ( Brunton et al., 2016 ) . Neural ordinary differential equations instead parameterize continuous-time dynamics through trainable vector fields ( Chen et al., 2018 ) . Active identification provides guarantees for nonlinear dynamics linear in known features ( Mania et al., 2022 ) , and continuous-time sampling theory characterizes when sampled evolution determines its generator ( Zeng et al., 2024 ) . These methods and results answer different parts of the recovery problem. Our formulation makes the target domain, sensor uncertainty, executable interventions, and acquisition costs explicit within a common analysis. The starting point is thus the experimental record, before selecting a representation or optimizer. An apparatus supplies a catalog of operations: preparing states, applying specified inputs, observing at chosen times, and, when available, calibrating against a reference. A learner may choose the next operation using earlier readings. Every operation has a cost, and the complete record must fit an acquisition budget. The central difficulty is whether this record separates candidate laws to the required physical precision. This perspective permits limits that apply to every learning algorithm, together with constructions that show when those limits can be approached. Information theory provides a useful language for separating the demands of the target from the abilities of the apparatus ( Shannon, 1948 ; Shannon, 1959 ; Cover and Thomas, 2006 ) . A law class may contain many physically different possibilities at a given resolution; describing the correct one requires information. Experiments deliver information through their responses. In the equal-prior two-law example, identifying the correct candidate requires one bit, but the circular experiment reveals none of it. The release can reveal that distinction. With a continuous law class, metric entropy and rate–distortion quantify the corresponding description requirement, while experimental information capacity describes what can be learned within the budget. There is an essential difference from ordinary communication. An experimenter does not know the true law and cannot encode it freely into a channel input. The experimenter can only probe the unknown world using available operations. Consequently, an inequality comparing required and available information is a necessary condition; it does not alone construct a successful recovery procedure. We give a separate response-matching decoder based on a finite collection of representative worlds. Under the stated compactness and continuity assumptions, arbitrary uniform accuracy is possible exactly when every pair of different target laws can be separated by some permitted experiment. The separating program may depend on the requested precision. Accuracy also depends on how strongly responses separate. Closely spaced responses require more repetitions in noise, and a small response error can correspond to a large physical-law error. Our analysis uses established tools from minimax information bounds, sequential experimental design, and inverse-problem stability ( Yang and Barron, 1999 ; Yu, 1997 ; Chernoff, 1959 ; Kaufmann et al., 2016 ; Donoho and Liu, 1991 ; Donoho, 1994 ) . For a concrete class of Lipschitz fields, we then quantify how preparation, readout, and elapsed time determine acquisition cost. The squared-error exponent − 2 / ( d + 4 ) -2/(d+4) is already established for nonparametric ODE estimation under specified observation designs ( Schötz, 2026 ; Schötz and Siebel, 2026 ) ; our costed access model examines it with adaptive experiment selection and contrasts state observations with direct field observations. The argument proceeds in this order. Section 2 defines the physical target and available experiments. Section 3 asks which laws those experiments can separate. Section 4 compares description requirements with accessible information, and Section 5 constructs a decoder and explains its stability. Section 6 specializes the theory to acquisition costs for Lipschitz dynamics. Section 7 returns to the orbital example and adds calibration and noisy-estimation cases.
